pedagogy.summary: This lower-KS2 topic makes the skeleton specific: children name and locate at least six major bones/groups — skull, spine (vertebrae), ribcage, pelvis, femur (thigh), humerus (upper arm) — and articulate the skeleton's three jobs (support, protection, movement). It also widens the lens: not all animals have an INTERNAL skeleton like ours — some have shells or an EXOSKELETON (insects, crabs), and some (worms) have no bony skeleton at all — so 'skeleton' means the structure that supports and protects, which can sit inside or out. Teach the naming on the child's OWN body (find your femur, feel your spine's vertebrae) and by labelling a skeleton diagram, then attach each bone to a job (femur supports your weight; skull protects the brain; humerus moves your arm with muscles). The scientific names are new vocabulary worth using precisely, paired with the everyday name. Keep function tied to specific bones, and use the animal comparison to generalise the idea of a skeleton.
bestPractices: Name bones on the child's own body AND on a diagram — locate your femur, feel the vertebrae down your spine — so names attach to felt locations, not just labels.
Pair each scientific name with its everyday name and its JOB (femur = thigh bone, supports your weight; humerus = upper-arm bone, moves the arm), so vocabulary and function are learned together.
Teach the three jobs as a lens applied to specific bones (which bones support? which protect? which move?), rather than as three abstract words.
Use the internal-vs-external comparison (insects/crabs have exoskeletons; snails have shells; worms have neither) to generalise 'skeleton' beyond human bones.
Reinforce with active labelling/sorting and precise vocabulary use; keep to major bones (not every bone) at this age.
keyRepresentations: Labelled human skeleton with the six target bones (skull, spine, ribcage, pelvis, femur, humerus)
Scientific-name / everyday-name / job triples for each bone
The three-jobs lens mapped onto specific bones (support/protect/move)
Internal skeleton vs exoskeleton vs shell comparison across animals
The child's own body as a locating map (find and feel each bone)
commonMisconceptions: 'All animals have bones inside like us' — missing exoskeletons (insects/crabs) and animals with no bony skeleton (worms).
'The spine is one single bone' — it's a column of many vertebrae, which is why it bends.
'Scientific bone names are interchangeable/decorative' — femur and humerus name specific bones, not any big/arm bone.
'The ribcage is solid armour' — it's a cage of curved bones that also moves for breathing.
'Bigger animals have more bones' — no simple size–count relationship; focus on structure and function.
'The skeleton only helps movement' — forgetting support and protection as equally important jobs.

learn.summary: Lower-KS2 learners name and locate at least six major bones/groups on their own body and on a diagram — skull, spine (vertebrae), ribcage, pelvis, femur (thigh bone), humerus (upper-arm bone) — pairing each scientific name with its everyday name and its job. They tie the skeleton's three jobs (support, protection, movement) to specific bones, then widen the idea of 'skeleton' using an internal-vs-external animal comparison: vertebrates have internal skeletons (usually bone; sharks' are cartilage), arthropods (insects, crabs) have exoskeletons, snails have shells, and worms have no bony or hard skeleton at all.

activities.title: Find it on you, then label it
feedback: If a learner feels only one hard ridge down the back, guide them to feel the bumps one after another: the spine is a column of many vertebrae, which is why it can bend.
If a learner uses a scientific name loosely (e.g. calls any large bone a femur), point back to the felt location: the femur is the single long bone between hip and knee.
Confirm success when the learner locates all six on their body and matches each to the correct spot and name on the diagram.
activities.rationale: Naming on the child's own body and on a diagram attaches new vocabulary to felt locations; the national curriculum expects pupils to identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement, and locating and naming the major bones builds on that requirement.
sourceClaims: Y3 pupils should identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement.
learnerActions: On your own body, locate and feel each target bone: run a finger down your spine to feel the separate vertebrae, press your ribcage, find the femur (thigh bone), the humerus (upper arm), the pelvis (hips) and the skull.
On a labelled human skeleton diagram, place or write the name for each of the six bones/groups: skull, spine (vertebrae), ribcage, pelvis, femur, humerus.
For each bone, say aloud the scientific name AND the everyday name together (e.g. 'femur — thigh bone'; 'humerus — upper-arm bone').

(Optional) If using an interactive skeleton, tap each bone to reveal its scientific name, everyday name and job — this is a convenience, not the thing that teaches the names; the felt location on your own body is the anchor.
activities.intendedInsight: Scientific bone names attach to real, felt locations on your own body, not just to labels on a picture; femur and humerus name specific bones, not any big or arm bone.

activities.title: Match each bone to its job
feedback: If a learner names only support, prompt: 'What protects your brain? What lets your arm move?' to surface protection and movement.
If a learner thinks the ribcage is solid armour, note it is a cage of curved bones that also moves as you breathe.
Confirm success when the learner gives all three jobs with at least one specific bone example each.
activities.rationale: Teaching the three jobs as a lens on specific bones (rather than three abstract words) ties function to anatomy; the curriculum frames the skeleton as being for support, protection and movement.
sourceClaims: Y3 pupils should identify that humans and some other animals have skeletons and muscles for support, protection and movement.
learnerActions: Match or write the job of each bone: which bones SUPPORT (hold the body up and give it shape), which PROTECT organs, and which enable MOVEMENT with muscles.
Give a worked example for each job: femur supports your weight; skull protects the brain; ribcage protects the heart and lungs; humerus moves your arm when muscles pull on it.
Notice that some bones do more than one job, and name all three jobs rather than only 'holding you up'.

(Optional) If using an interactive skeleton, a 'three jobs' filter can recolour bones to show at a glance which ones SUPPORT, which PROTECT and which MOVE — treat this as a sorting aid, then still state the job in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: The skeleton has three important jobs — support, protection AND movement — and each can be tied to specific bones with examples.

activities.title: Do all animals have bones inside?
feedback: If a learner says the crab has bones inside and the shell is just extra armour, correct it: the hard outer casing IS the skeleton (an exoskeleton), doing the support and protection jobs from the outside.
If a learner says a shell or exoskeleton does nothing a skeleton does, match the jobs across designs: it supports and protects just like your bones, only from outside.

Extend thinking: ask what problem a worm faces with no bony skeleton at all, or why a crab has to shed its exoskeleton and grow a new one as it gets bigger (whereas a snail's shell grows along with the snail).
activities.rationale: The internal-vs-external comparison generalises the idea of a skeleton beyond human bones and directly addresses the 'all animals have bones inside' misconception.
sourceClaims: Animals have different skeleton types — vertebrates have an internal bony skeleton (endoskeleton), arthropods (insects, crabs) have an external exoskeleton, and some animals have hydrostatic or no bony skeleton.
learnerActions: Compare animals by how their body is held up and protected: a beetle or crab has a hard OUTER casing (an exoskeleton); a snail has a shell; a worm has no bony skeleton inside or out.
Sort several animals into groups: internal skeleton, exoskeleton, shell, or no hard skeleton.

Explain what is the SAME and what is DIFFERENT between a crab's exoskeleton and your skeleton (same jobs — support, protection and movement with muscles attached; different design — outside versus inside).

(Optional) A lift-the-flap 'do all animals have a skeleton like mine?' reveal — e.g. a beetle wearing its skeleton on the outside and a snail's shell — can prompt the comparison, but any side-by-side comparison serves the same goal.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Skeleton' means the structure that supports and protects a body, which can sit inside or outside; not all animals have internal bones like ours.

activities.title: Build-and-name self-check
feedback: For a mislabelled bone, send the learner back to feel the location on their own body before retrying.
For a mis-sorted animal, ask where its support and protection come from — inside or outside.

This is recognition/placement practice: a correct match shows the learner can pick the right label, but does not by itself show they can explain why, so also have the learner explain a choice in their own words.
activities.rationale: Active labelling and sorting with instant self-check turn naming into practice and can double as consolidation; keep to major bones (not every bone) at this age.
learnerActions: Assemble or label a skeleton by dragging/writing each bone name onto the correct bone, then check against the correct placement.
Match each bone to its job (support / protect / move).
Categorise a set of animals by skeleton type (internal / exoskeleton / shell / no hard skeleton) and check your sorting.
activities.intendedInsight: Active labelling and sorting can consolidate precise naming and the internal/external distinction, and can reveal any remaining gaps.

constraints: Keep to the six major bones/groups (skull, spine/vertebrae, ribcage, pelvis, femur, humerus) at this age — do not require every bone in the body.
Always pair the scientific name with the everyday name so vocabulary and meaning are learned together.

Tap-to-reveal, drag-the-label and sorting formats are recognition/placement practice; they can teach and check naming and classification but do not by themselves elicit an explanation, so also ask learners to explain a bone's job or the inside/outside difference in their own words.
A rotatable 3D skeleton can help locate bones in the round (e.g. pelvis position, spine curvature) but is optional — naming and function are fully served by a 2D diagram and the child's own body.
Treat the diagram and any screen model as representations; the felt locations on the learner's own body are the anchor for the vocabulary.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row marked a conversation/dialogue format as 'poor' for this naming task; that is a catalog fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law, so it is omitted rather than asserted as a universal limit on dialogue teaching.
The exoskeleton source claim (Britannica) is marked verified:false in the row; the internal/external comparison rests on it and has not been re-checked here.

The source claim notes some animals have hydrostatic skeletons (e.g. worms); activities simplify this to 'no bony skeleton', which is age-appropriate but is an approximation, not independently re-verified.

Original text framed a 'moment of insight' as tied to a specific flap interaction; this has been reframed as a learning goal reachable by any comparison activity, with the flap/recolour/tap interactions retained only as optional examples, not mandatory mechanisms.

probeDeeper: Which of your bones protects your brain? Which protect your heart and lungs?
A worm has no skeleton inside OR outside. What problem does that create for a worm that you don't have?
Why might an animal with its skeleton on the OUTSIDE have to shed it and grow a new one as it gets bigger?
assess.correctAnswer: A crab and beetle don't have bones inside — they have a hard outer casing called an exoskeleton that supports and protects them from the outside; your skeleton does similar jobs but is on the INSIDE. The three jobs of your skeleton are support (holding your body up and giving it shape), protection (the skull protects the brain, the ribcage protects the heart and lungs), and movement (bones work with muscles). Same jobs, different design — inside versus outside.

errorPatterns.pattern: All animals have bones inside like us — a crab has bones inside its shell.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce the exoskeleton as a hard OUTER casing that replaces internal bones; the shell IS the skeleton, on the outside.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the crab has bones inside, and its shell is just extra armour on top.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the crab or insect has an internal skeleton under its shell.

errorPatterns.pattern: The skeleton's only job is to hold you up (misses protection and movement).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add the other two jobs with examples — skull/ribs protecting organs, bones plus muscles for movement.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names only support; omits protecting organs and enabling movement.

errorPatterns.pattern: A shell or exoskeleton isn't a skeleton at all and does nothing a skeleton does.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Match the jobs across designs: the exoskeleton supports and protects just like your bones, only from outside.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies the exoskeleton supports or protects the animal.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks all animals have internal bones, or names only 'holding you up' as the skeleton's job.
responseLevels.full: Names and locates major bones, gives all three functions with examples, and contrasts internal skeletons with exoskeletons — reasoning about an animal with neither.
responseLevels.partial: Names bones and some functions, but can't cleanly give all three jobs, or is unsure about internal versus external skeletons.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A crab and a beetle are hard on the OUTSIDE, but you are soft on the outside and hard on the inside. Do they have bones like you, just in a different place? What is the same and what is different about how their bodies are held up — and what are the THREE jobs your own skeleton does?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who assumes all animals have internal bones, or who names only 'holding you up', reveals the gap. Only a child who contrasts internal and external skeletons AND gives all three functions answers fully. The tier-two 'same and different' forces the internal/external distinction rather than a rote bone list.
